title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is filled with infinite stars, why isn't the whole sky as bright as the sun?
summary: A simple observation—the darkness of the night sky—turns out to encode deep truths about the age, finitude, and expansion of the universe.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. The sky is dark, dotted with a few thousand visible stars. This seems utterly unremarkable—until you consider the implications of an infinite, unchanging universe filled with infinite stars. In that case, every single line of sight from your eye should eventually terminate on the surface of a star. The night sky should be a wall of blinding light, as bright as the sun's surface, not a black canvas with pinpricks of light. This is Olbers' Paradox, and its resolution reshaped our understanding of the cosmos.

The Simple Argument

Imagine the universe as infinite and static, uniformly filled with stars. Draw a sphere of radius r around Earth: the number of stars in that shell grows with r², but each star's apparent brightness falls off as 1/r². Those two effects cancel exactly, so every shell of space, no matter how distant, contributes the same total amount of light to the sky. Add up infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness. Even accounting for stars blocking other stars, the entire sky should glow like a stellar surface. Yet at night, it's dark. Something in the simple assumptions must be wrong.

The Resolution: A Universe With a Birthday

The paradox dissolves once you drop the assumption that the universe is infinitely old and static. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, and light travels at a finite speed. We can only see stars whose light has had time to reach us—a finite "observable universe." Beyond a certain distance, there simply hasn't been enough time since the Big Bang for light to arrive yet. The night sky is dark not because there aren't enough stars, but because most of the universe is invisible to us, hidden behind the wall of time itself.

Expansion compounds the effect: light from the most distant visible objects has been redshifted by the expansion of space into wavelengths we can't see with the naked eye, and the cosmic microwave background—the actual "wall" predicted by the paradox—does exist, just not as visible light. It arrives as faint microwave radiation, the afterglow of a hot, young universe now stretched and cooled by billions of years of expansion.

Why a Children's Question Became a Cosmological Proof

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is that it's a purely qualitative observation—the sky is dark—that constrains the deepest properties of the universe: its age, its finitude in time, and its expansion. Long before telescopes could measure redshift or satellites could detect the cosmic microwave background, the simple darkness of the night sky was already telling us that the universe could not be infinite, eternal, and static all at once. It was one of the first pieces of evidence that the universe has a history, not just a structure.

A Deceptively Deep Question

The paradox is often credited to Heinrich Olbers in 1823, though Kepler and others raised versions of it centuries earlier, each drawing different conclusions—Kepler used it to argue the universe must be finite in space. It's a reminder that some of the most powerful scientific insights come not from exotic experiments but from taking an everyday observation seriously enough to ask why it isn't stranger than it is.

perspectives.title: Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite speed of light means we see distant stars as they were long ago; the deepest reaches of space are simply too far for their light to have arrived yet.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The universe's finite age (~13.8 billion years) and its expansion redshift distant starlight out of the visible spectrum, converting what would be blinding light into the cosmic microwave background.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler, Halley, and Olbers all wrestled with this puzzle centuries before modern cosmology existed, each interpretation revealing the assumptions their eras held about infinity and eternity.

perspectives.title: Philosophical Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox shows how a single mundane observation, reasoned through rigorously, can falsify entire cosmological models—evidence doesn't have to be exotic to be powerful.
